title: KV-cache + micro-batch policy: tokenization-aware latency vs fidelity evaluation
creator: Ananya Rao
description:
Background: Recent config proposals introduce a tokenization-aware KV cache invalidation and a 'micro-batch' policy that groups short requests to improve GPU utilization. Both changes promise lower cost per token but may alter generation fidelity for some prompts (especially short-prompts and chat turn boundaries).

Goal: Define, run, and document a reproducible eval harness that quantifies the latency and quality trade-offs across the new tokenization-aware KV cache settings and several micro-batch thresholds. Produce clear pass/fail criteria for rollout and a lightweight regression monitor to run as part of the nightly eval job.

Scope: Cover 3 model families (open-llama-13b, redwood-mini-7b, and a smaller customer-sim model variant), 4 KV-cache modes (none, conservative, tokenization-aware, aggressive), and 5 micro-batch thresholds (1, 8, 32, 64, 128). Evaluate at representative sequence length distributions: short-chat (mean 40 tokens), instruction-heavy (mean 120 tokens), and long-context (mean 1024 tokens).

Non-goal: This ticket does not implement rollout automation or autoscaling changes. It focuses on eval data, metrics, and regression detection logic.
acceptance_criteria: A reproducible harness that runs combos of (model × cache-mode × micro-batch) and emits latency P50/P95 and quality deltas vs baseline
Quality is measured by a blend: BLEU-like ngram for deterministic tasks, and automatic embedding-based similarity plus human-annotated rating sample for open generation
A documented threshold table specifying acceptable quality degradation per customer tier (e.g., <1.0% absolute decrease for P0 routes, <3.0% for P2) together with latency improvement targets
A CI job that executes a trimmed subset nightly and raises an alert when any config causes quality regression beyond threshold or latency regression beyond SLO
Clear runbook section describing how to interpret false positives from tokenization changes and how to rollback a rollout
steps: Design dataset: compose 1.5k prompts across short-chat, instruction, and long-context buckets (mix of synthetic + anonymized production prompts)
Implement harness: extend existing eval runner to support incremental KV cache toggles and per-request micro-batching simulation
Instrumentation: record per-request generation tokens, kv-hit-rate, GPU utilization, P50/P95 latency, and deterministic seeds for replay
Quality evaluation: run automatic metrics and sample 200 responses per config for quick human rating via internal annotation queue
Run matrix: execute full matrix for models on staging infra, collect metrics to the eval dashboard
Nightly regression: wire a trimmed nightly job (most-opposite pairs) and configure alerting criteria in Opsgenie/Slack
Report: produce a one-page recommendation and rollout guardrails for PM/Infra review
comments: 2026-02-21 - Ananya Rao: Initial ticket created after discussion with Runtime and Evals teams. Added scope and proposed matrices.
2026-02-25 - Liam Chen: Implemented harness prototype; can toggle kv-mode per request. Pushed branch to github: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/2876
2026-03-01 - Review (PM - Marissa): Asked to include explicit customer-tier thresholds and to validate short-chat prompts more thoroughly. Added acceptance criteria for P0/P2 tiers.

2026-03-05 - Design feedback (Diego): Recommend adding token-boundary mismatch checks; some tokenization-aware cache configs may shift tokenization of newlines leading to off-by-one contexts. Added instrumentation task.

2026-03-09 - Liam Chen: Completed first full sweep on staging for redwood-mini-7b. Early signals: micro-batch=32 reduces P95 by ~18% but shows 1.6% drop in embedding-similarity on short-chat. Attached summary: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/EVALS/KVCache+Microbatch+Sweep
notes: Initial human annotation suggests most quality drops are concentrated in short-chat turn resets when tokenization-aware cache omits a newline token. We should evaluate a hybrid invalidation rule that forces cache boundary at any speaker-change token. Planning a quick follow-up experiment if the hybrid rule reduces failures without hurting latency gains.
implementation_risks: Tokenization drift: different tokenizers or version mismatches can make cached KV entries invalid and induce silent quality regressions
Measurement noise: micro-batching depends on runtime arrival patterns; staging synthetic arrival may overestimate latency benefits
Human label scale: to catch 1% absolute regressions at 95% confidence we may need more annotation than budgeted
